The reality of a taser is that, yes, it sucks, but it's using an electrical current to interrupt your body's control of its voluntary muscle movement for just a few short seconds, and in the overwhelming majority of cases, it does nothing more than that, and aside from two small pinpricks from the probes, it's done and over with in less than 10 seconds. There's no broken bones, lacerations, ruptured organs, bruising, or soft tissue damage. There's a few seconds of tightly and painfully tensed muscles - sort of like a full-body Charlie horse - and the temporary physical exhaustion that follows.

If the police are using fists, feet, or batons to gain compliance...they're punching or kicking someone, or hitting them with a steel pipe. Shattered bones, damaged joints, significant lacerations, bruising, internal bleeding...Even permanent effects such as nerve damage, blindness, or death. An officer could easily be aiming a strike at the meaty upper portion of the arm and the suspect might duck or dodge to avoid the blow, and the baton impacts the side of their head, killing them or causing very severe injury. Hi /v/writing!

I never had this problem in all my years of writing, but lately my short stories and novel chapters are rushing trough the plot and character development trough dialogue and infodump and I feel like I need to 'slow down' and add some more sensory description of the settings the characters are in to fully submerge the reader in the scene.

I have my characters and plot and world pretty thought-out, but when I'm writing I feel like most environmental details aren't directly adding to the story, unless I can use it as vocalised object (from the point of view from the main character, to emphasise his or her mood) or if it's important information about the history of the world or characters.

Right now I'm just going to pick up a book and analyse how sensory description and environmental details are being woven in to the story and if they are 'adding' to the plot or setting or just there for fluff.

How do you guys weave environment into your stories? Do you use sensory or static descritpion? Do you ever write out the basic plot and then go back and add all sorts of details to the scene?
What are your ground rules for sensory and/or environment description?

Disclaimer: Everything that follows is just my opinion. Writing is first and foremost a self-study, where finding answers isn't as simple as, "this is right, and this is wrong."

When writing environmental descriptions, looking at the perspective of the story and how the environment interacts with characters determines how important description is. Perspective acts as a divining rod for what pieces of the environment are more than simply set-dressing. In first, second, and third-person omniscient, determining these parts of the environment are a bit more seamless to write about as the character is directly noting their existence. However, in non-omniscient third-person, the narrator is separate is some way to the characters in the story, thereby making description of the scene a delicate balancing act between fluff and useful sensory information.

Interaction comes into play via characters interacting with things and things interacting with characters. The former is straight-forward, a character does something that results in sensory description of something in the world. The latter however, requires a bit more thought as things interacting with characters is not simply limited to tripping over a rock or being chased by a boulder. People look at the world through a complex pattern of historic and emotional ideas, wherein looking at a tree can just be that or more; this is equally true with characters. Walking down a dirt road can be something simple, or it can be a trip down memory lane for the character in question. Description of interactions from this can not only give you interesting sensory information, but help create a more diverse character.

Thanks for your reply!

I've been looking at my work and I figured out that most environmental information is more or less a prompt to describe the inner-workings and history of the world it's set in (fantasy) or the history and memories of the main character. So most of the descriptions have the function of conveying information rather than a setting, emotion or senses. I think it would work best if there is a combination of the two to make the reader submerge more into the world. As always, it's just going back into the text and rewriting and editing these parts.

At least (I think) I know what the main concerns with my writing are at this moment. I think it's rooted in the fact that I've been writing short stories for years and these are my first novel chapters. In short stories all your descriptions, all your words, need to be accounted for. So I need to practice the fluff part. I write in non-participating third person narrative.

No problem. Personally though, I wouldn't ignore that voice that you've developed from writing short stories. Even in novels, every word should still be accounted for. Words and sentences have as much impact as paragraphs and pages when it comes to description. It about using the right words for the moment. Sometimes the right words aren't there, and that is when a greater number of words must be substituted in, but novels no more need fluff than any other prose. Use the amount of words you feel is right for what you're talking about. and if someone tells you that you're shy of a word-count, screw the word-count.
